newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina clings to Falkland hopes under Labour.
newsitem.headline: Argentina clings to Falkland hopes under Labour.

text.p: Labour's victory in British elections raised the Argentine government's hopes on Friday for its claim to sovereignty of the Falklands, but the press and political opposition called such optimism "utopic."

The Peronist government's expectations of good news on the Falkland Islands have grown as the Labour Party's chances of a win rose, forcing Labour to issue a statement last week saying there was "not a shred of truth" in such suggestions.

But President Carlos Menem, who has worked on closer ties with Britain while insisting he will win back the islands Argentina calls the Malvinas by 2000, has chosen to ignore Labour's warnings there will be no change in policy.

Menem sent Labour leader Tony Blair congratulations with no mention of the dispute, but said in comments published on Friday: "One always maintains the hope that a change of government and orientation in that country could be positive in some way for our sovereignty claim."
"Maybe what I have said for some time -- that Argentine flags will fly in the islands by the year 2000 -- will now be fulfilled without wars or anything like that," Menem said.
Deputy Foreign Minister Andres Cisneros, addressing the cynics, told Reuters: "It is unthinkable that any such historic moment will not bring changes."

Argentina says the windswept South Atlantic islands were "usurped" by Britain in 1833. In 1982, a military government sent troops to enforce that claim, leading to a 10-week war with Britain in which 1,000 servicemen died.
Argentina has now been a democracy since 1983 and trade and diplomatic links with Britain are flourishing.

But the scars of the lost war are still sore, evident in ceremonies on Friday for the 15th anniversary of the war's most lethal engagement -- the sinking of the warship General Belgrano by a British submarine with 323 lives lost.

Conservative Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, who led Britain into war, and her successor John Major refused even to discuss sovereignty. The only concession from the islanders, mistrustful of Argentina, was to allow visits to war graves.

All the signs are that the Labour government will not see things differently. "My party's position has always been that at the end of the day it will be the islanders who decide if there will be a change in sovereignty or not," the party's Latin American spokesman Tony Lloyd said recently.

Hence La Nacion newspaper's verdict that Blair will mean "Just a change of style" and a column in Clarin saying "the idea that Blair's rise to power could mean major changes to London's position on the Malvinas is, for now, a utopia."
Rodolfo Terragno, leader of the opposition Radical Party, said by phone from London where he was observing the elections that it would be "naive" to expect changes on the Falklands.

"When the Conservatives' have been warning that Labour will surrender British interests, Labour can't take unilateral moves," said Terragno. "If anything changes on the Malvinas it will be because Argentina changes its unintelligent policies."
He said Argentina had "naively expected the solution to come from the United States or the islanders or Tony Blair," whereas it should be lobbying harder in the United Nations.

Argentina has taken heart from Britain's imminent handover of Hong Kong to China. "Sooner or later, Britain must accept what the U.N. has demanded since 1965, and do the same as it will do in Hong Kong in June, which is to put an end to its territorial situations all over the world," said Cisneros.
